summary: Psalm 78 opens by calling the people to hear old instruction and pass it to future generations. It then retells Israel’s repeated pattern: God rescues, provides, judges rebellion, shows mercy, and brings his people onward. The chapter ends by moving from the rejection of Ephraim and Shiloh to God’s choice of Judah, Zion, and David as shepherd of Israel.
whyItMatters: This chapter shows how historical memory works inside the Psalms: the past is retold to teach trust, obedience, and honest recognition of failure. In Book III of Psalms, it also helps explain the importance of sanctuary, tribe, and shepherding leadership without pretending Israel’s story was simple.

context.author: The heading says, “A contemplation by Asaph.” In Psalms, headings are ancient parts of the received collection, but their exact force can mean authorship, association, dedication, or belonging.
context.audience: Israel’s worshiping and instructed community, especially a generation being taught to remember and pass on what God had done.
context.date: Psalms is an anthology formed over time; individual poems may preserve material from the monarchy through the postexilic period. This psalm retells Israel’s past through David’s selection without identifying its own date of composition.
context.setting: The chapter looks back over Israel’s story from Egypt and the wilderness to settlement, Shiloh, Zion, and David.
context.literaryForm: Historical remembrance in Hebrew poetry, using repeated contrasts between God’s deeds and the people’s forgetfulness, rebellion, and partial return.

outline.heading: A call to teach memory
outline.note: The speaker summons the people to listen and says the story must be told to coming generations so they will hope in God and not repeat stubborn rebellion.

outline.heading: Forgetting after rescue
outline.note: Ephraim is named as turning back, and the poem recalls God’s deeds in Egypt, at the sea, in the cloud and fire, and at the rocks in the wilderness.

outline.heading: Provision met by unbelief
outline.note: The people rebel, question whether God can feed them, and receive manna and meat; their craving is followed by judgment.

outline.heading: False return and divine mercy
outline.note: Even after judgment the people keep sinning; when they seek God their words are unreliable, but God remembers their frailty and restrains destruction.

outline.heading: Egypt remembered again
outline.note: The psalm repeats the charge that they forgot God’s hand, then recounts signs in Egypt, the firstborn struck, the people led like sheep, and the nations driven out before them.

outline.heading: Shiloh abandoned
outline.note: After entering the land, the people again rebel through high places and images, and the poem describes God abandoning Shiloh and giving his people over to defeat and grief.

outline.heading: Judah, Zion, and David chosen
outline.note: The Lord rises against his adversaries, rejects Joseph and Ephraim, chooses Judah and Mount Zion, and brings David from the sheepfolds to shepherd Israel.

keyVerses.text: We will not hide them from their children, telling to the generation to come the praises of Yahweh, his strength, and his wondrous deeds that he has done.
keyVerses.why: This states the chapter’s purpose: remembered acts of God are to be taught across generations.

keyVerses.text: because they didn’t believe in God, and didn’t trust in his salvation.
keyVerses.why: This verse summarizes the inner problem behind the wilderness complaints: the issue is not lack of evidence but lack of trust.

keyVerses.text: But he, being merciful, forgave iniquity, and didn’t destroy them. Yes, many times he turned his anger away, and didn’t stir up all his wrath.
keyVerses.why: This anchors the chapter’s repeated contrast between real rebellion and restrained judgment.

keyVerses.text: So he was their shepherd according to the integrity of his heart, and guided them by the skillfulness of his hands.
keyVerses.why: The final verse presents David’s rule as shepherding, closing the chapter’s long movement from failed memory to chosen leadership.

questions.question: Why does the chapter begin by talking about children and future generations?
questions.answer: The opening says the story is not to be hidden from children but told to “the generation to come.” The goal is practical memory: future generations are to set their hope in God, remember God’s deeds, and keep his commandments. The chapter’s long retelling is therefore instruction, not merely nostalgia.

questions.question: What is a “parable” here?
questions.answer: Verse 2 says the speaker will open his mouth “in a parable” and utter “dark sayings of old.” In this chapter, that does not introduce a short fictional story; it introduces a reflective retelling of Israel’s past meant to teach. The old events are presented so the hearers can understand a pattern in their own history.

questions.question: Who are the “children of Ephraim,” and why are they mentioned?
questions.answer: Verse 9 says the children of Ephraim were armed but turned back in battle, and verses 67-68 later say God rejected the tent of Joseph, did not choose Ephraim, and chose Judah. The chapter uses Ephraim as part of its contrast between failed leadership or faithfulness and God’s later choice of Judah and Zion. Readers differ on the precise historical incident behind verse 9; the chapter itself emphasizes covenant failure and forgetting God’s deeds.

questions.question: Why does the psalm retell the wilderness food story in such detail?
questions.answer: The food story shows the tension that drives much of the chapter. The people ask whether God can prepare a table in the wilderness, even after seeing water from the rock. God provides manna and meat, but the chapter says their craving and unbelief remain, so provision does not automatically produce trust.

questions.question: Does the chapter say their return to God was sincere?
questions.answer: The chapter gives a mixed and sobering picture. Verses 34-35 say they returned, sought God earnestly, and remembered God as rock and redeemer. But verses 36-37 immediately say they flattered him, lied with their tongue, and were not faithful in his covenant.

questions.question: How can the chapter speak of God’s anger and mercy together?
questions.answer: Psalm 78 does not soften either side. It repeatedly says God was angry at rebellion, unbelief, and idolatry. It also says God was merciful, forgave iniquity, remembered human frailty, and did not stir up all his wrath.

questions.question: What are the signs in Egypt doing in this chapter?
questions.answer: The signs in Egypt are recalled as evidence of God’s power and of the people’s failure to remember. The chapter lists rivers turned to blood, flies, frogs, ruined crops, hail, pestilence, and the striking of the firstborn. The point is not to give a complete prose history but to place rescue and judgment inside Israel’s remembered story.

questions.question: What is the “tent of Shiloh,” and why is its abandonment important?
questions.answer: Verse 60 says God abandoned the tent of Shiloh, the tent he had placed among men. The following verses describe defeat, captivity, sword, and grief, so Shiloh marks a severe loss connected with Israel’s rebellion. The chapter then turns from that rejected site toward Judah, Mount Zion, and David.

questions.question: Is the final focus on David mainly about power or care?
questions.answer: The chapter ends with David, but it describes him through shepherd language. God takes him from sheepfolds and brings him to shepherd Jacob and Israel. The final line highlights integrity of heart and skillfulness of hands, so leadership is pictured as guided care, not only royal status.

glossary.def: A word in the heading for this psalm; here it introduces a reflective poem that teaches by remembering Israel’s past.
A binding relationship or obligation named in the chapter when God appoints teaching in Israel and when the people fail to remain faithful.
The food from the sky that God gives in the wilderness when the people question whether he can provide bread.
The place whose tent God abandons in the chapter’s account of judgment and loss before the poem turns to Zion.
A care-and-guidance image used for God leading his people and for David’s leadership over Jacob and Israel.
